articles.heading: Round Robin System
articles.content:
In a round-robin tournament every player meets every other player. The most common forms are:
- Single Round Robin: each player meets every other player once
- Double Round Robin: each player meets every other player twice

The Berger table (also called Scheveningen table in team contexts) is used for scheduling. In a single round-robin with n players:
- If n is even: there are n-1 rounds and n/2 games per round
- If n is odd: there are n rounds and (n-1)/2 games per round, with one player receiving a bye each round

The round-robin is considered the fairest system, as every player faces exactly the same set of opponents.

In team round-robins, the Berger table assigns which team plays White on Board 1 in each round. The result is typically determined by match points (number of matches won) and game points (total individual game results) as tiebreaks.

The round-robin system requires n×(n-1)/2 total games for n players, making it impractical for large fields. It is typically used in elite round-robin events, invitational tournaments, and zonal championships.

articles.heading: Swiss System
articles.content:
In a Swiss system tournament, players are paired against opponents with equal or similar scores. No player is ever eliminated. The Swiss system was first used in Zurich, Switzerland in 1895.

Key characteristics:
- Players are never paired against the same opponent twice
- Players receive colour allocations as close to alternating as possible
- The number of rounds is far fewer than the number of players needed for a round-robin
- After each round, players are grouped into score brackets and paired within brackets

Swiss tournaments are suitable for large numbers of players where a full round-robin is impractical. A typical Swiss event has between 7 and 11 rounds regardless of whether there are 50 or 500 players.

FIDE uses the Dutch System as the standard Swiss pairing system. The Baku Acceleration is an approved accelerated variant. Computer-generated pairings using FIDE-approved software (such as Swiss Manager or Vega) are considered official.

The winner of a Swiss tournament is determined by total score. Tiebreak systems (Buchholz, Sonneborn-Berger, number of wins, etc.) are used to separate players on equal scores.

articles.heading: Scheveningen System
articles.content:
In the Scheveningen system, two teams play each other with every member of one team playing every member of the other team. If Team A has n players and Team B has m players, the total number of games is n × m.

The system is named after the Dutch resort where it was first used in 1923. It is most commonly used when two national teams or club teams meet in a test match.

Board pairings can be determined:
- By rating order (highest-rated player on Board 1)
- By drawing of lots
- By other pre-announced criteria

The Scheveningen system ensures every player on one team faces every player on the other, giving a complete picture of the strength comparison between the teams.

In team events using the Scheveningen format, colour allocation across boards must be carefully managed so that each player receives approximately equal numbers of White and Black games across the match.

articles.heading: Schiller System
articles.content:
The Schiller system is a group-based tournament format. Players are divided into preliminary groups, each played as a round-robin. The top finishers from each group advance to a final phase, which may be another round-robin or a knockout.

This system balances the thoroughness of a round-robin with practicality for larger fields. It is common in youth and junior championships where a full round-robin is not feasible but a pure Swiss system is not considered appropriate.

The arbiter must ensure:
- Groups are composed fairly, typically by rating or seeding
- The number of qualifiers per group is announced in advance
- Tiebreak procedures for qualification from groups are established before the event begins

articles.heading: Skalitzka System
articles.content:
The Skalitzka system is designed for team tournaments where each team member plays one game against the corresponding board player of each opposing team.

Unlike the Scheveningen system (where every player plays every opponent), in the Skalitzka system Board 1 plays Board 1 of all other teams, Board 2 plays Board 2, and so on. This maintains equal board distribution and means every player competes in the same number of games regardless of field size.

The total number of games for a player equals (number of teams - 1). Results are aggregated both by board and by total team score.

This system is favoured in league-format team competitions where preserving board hierarchy across all rounds is important.

articles.heading: Matches
articles.content:
A match is a competition between two players or two teams over a fixed number of games. The result is determined by total points scored or by number of games won.

Match formats:
- Fixed number of games (e.g. World Championship: 14 games)
- First to reach a target score (e.g. first to 7.5 points wins)
- Games until a player leads by a specified margin

In case of a tie after the scheduled games, matches may continue with playoff games. The standard FIDE playoff sequence is:
1. Rapid games (equal time controls)
2. Blitz games if still tied
3. An Armageddon game if necessary

In an Armageddon game, White has more time but must win to advance. A draw counts as a win for Black. The player with Black in the Armageddon game is usually determined by drawing of lots or by giving the right to choose colour to one player who then faces a bidding system.

For team matches, the result is typically the total of all individual game points. If level, individual match results per board may serve as tiebreaks.

articles.heading: Knock-out System
articles.content:
In a knock-out (elimination) tournament, players or teams are eliminated after losing a match. The winner advances to the next round. This continues until only one player or team remains — the champion.

Formats:
- Single elimination: one loss and you are out
- Double elimination: a player must lose twice before elimination (less common in chess)
- Seeded draws: the highest-rated players are kept apart in the draw to meet only in later rounds

Knock-out tournaments require fewer rounds (log₂ of the number of players) but many participants are eliminated early with few games played. This format is used in:
- World Cup (Swiss qualifier + knockout)
- Grand Prix finals
- Club cup competitions
- Later stages of championships

The arbiter must pay special attention to tiebreak procedures within each match (rapid, blitz, Armageddon), ensuring all players are clearly informed of the procedures before each match begins. Time controls for each playoff stage must be specified in the tournament regulations.
